title: High-Mileage EV Overpricing: Root-Cause Investigation
summary: A pricing engine was systematically overpricing high-mileage EVs. This case study traces the issue from a first data pass to the exact line of buggy code, then designs a monitoring system to catch it automatically next time.
explanation: A pricing engine was flagged for overpricing high-mileage EVs: cases where the guaranteed price came in well above what the car actually sold for. This case study (built on a synthetic dataset, structured the way I'd approach a real production pricing-integrity investigation) walks through confirming the problem, narrowing down its source, finding the actual bug, and designing a way to catch it automatically next time.

Confirming the problem meant ruling out noise first. Segmenting by fuel type showed EVs alone carried a 6,655 DKK average spread versus -300 to 400 DKK for every other fuel type, and splitting EVs by mileage narrowed it further to high-mileage EVs specifically (13,857 DKK average spread vs -67 DKK for low-mileage EVs). From there, comparing the platform's automated "robot" pricing against human analyst pricing on the exact same high-mileage EVs isolated the actual source: the robot was off by 30,167 DKK per car, nearly 19x worse than analysts, and responsible for 93% of the total leakage from just 6 cars.

Reading the pricing script explained why. A flat 24,000 DKK (plus 14,000 DKK for Tesla or Polestar) gets added to every EV regardless of mileage, while the only correction is a small 0.18 DKK/km deduction above 80,000 km, so the higher the mileage, the further the price drifts from reality. A second, unrelated bug turned up along the way: the power penalty compares kilowatts against a horsepower threshold, silently under-penalizing high-power EVs.

The write-up closes with a monitoring design, not just a diagnosis: a weekly anomaly-detection function that builds rolling, per-segment control limits from each segment's own history, while explicitly excluding any week already flagged as anomalous, since otherwise a lasting bug quietly gets absorbed into its own baseline and the alerts go silent exactly when they're needed most.
highlights: Traced a ~194,000 DKK leakage on high-mileage EVs to one specific bug in the pricing script's mileage correction logic
Isolated the cause by comparing robot vs. analyst pricing on identical cars: found the automated pricing was 19x less accurate
Designed a production-style monitoring function with per-segment control limits and a flagged-week exclusion mechanism, so a lasting problem can't quietly become its own new normal
Communicated findings as a structured business memo, covering problem definition, method and reasoning per step, root cause, and an explicit limitations and open-questions section
